concept.name: Abstention
concept.definition: The design choice that lets a model decline to answer on inputs where it is likely to be wrong, trading coverage for accuracy. In selective classification (Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017), the system pairs a predictor with a selection function that rejects low-confidence instances so that a user-chosen risk level is met with high probability.
concept.intuition: A system allowed to say 'I don't know' can be far more trustworthy on the answers it does give — you choose how much silence to buy for how much accuracy.
concept.mechanics: A selection function g(x) (e.g., a confidence threshold) decides whether the predictor h(x) answers or abstains; selective risk is the loss measured only on answered instances, and coverage is the fraction answered. Raising the abstention threshold lowers risk but reduces coverage, tracing a risk-coverage curve used to pick an operating point.
concept.formula: Selective risk R(h, g) = E[ℓ(h(x), y) · g(x)] / E[g(x)]; coverage φ(h, g) = E[g(x)], where ℓ is the loss, h the predictor, and g ∈ {0,1} the selection (accept) function.
concept.failure_modes: Abstention quality depends on the confidence signal: an overconfident miscalibrated model abstains on the wrong cases and answers confidently where it is wrong. It also fails exactly on distribution shift, where inputs unlike anything in validation produce confident nonsense.
concept.misconceptions: Abstaining is not an admission the system is broken — it is a designed operating mode that converts unknown errors into visible non-answers. A high abstention rate is also not automatically good; it can hide a useless system that answers nothing.
concept.example: A trading-knowledge assistant abstains — 'no verified source available' — when asked for a contract specification absent from its knowledge library, instead of guessing a plausible tick value.

citations.source: Geifman & El-Yaniv, 'Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks' (NeurIPS 2017)
